tier_reason: BENCHMARKS.md gives per-VM tables against Wasmtime (cranelift, winch) and Wasmer singlepass with the CPU model (Threadripper 3970X), the exact commit 190ea5ac and replication steps; the harness is public (tools/benchtool: src/main.rs, src/backend/backend_*.rs, 01-build-benchmarks.sh, 02-run-benchmarks.rb, 03-analyze-benchmarks.rb), with toolchains pinned by rust-toolchain.toml files and flags in Cargo.toml and guest-programs/build-benchmarks.sh at that commit. I checked that PolkaVM's compile rows are not cache hits: the module-cache feature is off by default and benchtool does not enable it.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: At the benchmarked commit 190ea5ac: benchtool built with Rust 1.82.0 (tools/benchtool/rust-toolchain.toml; the workspace root pinned 1.75.0, and the 1.86.0 in the record is today's HEAD), cargo --release with lto = true, codegen-units = 1, debug = true; guest programs built with nightly-2024-11-01 (guest-programs/rust-toolchain.toml) by guest-programs/build-benchmarks.sh, Wasm guests with RUSTFLAGS '-C target-cpu=mvp -C target-feature=-sign-ext'; benchtool pins wasmtime 26.0.1 (default features off: cranelift, winch, runtime, so no parallel compilation and no cache), wasmer 5.0.0 (singlepass), wasmi 0.39.1, and a Go shim on wazero v1.8.1; 02-run-benchmarks.rb disables turbo boost, sets the performance governor and pins the run to CPUs 1-2 with a cgroup; criterion sample_size 10, mean estimate reported.
corrections.claimed_speedup: One-shot (compile + init + run) on pinky: PolkaVM 64-bit recompiler 55.408 ms vs Wasmtime (cranelift) 116.002 ms and Wasmer (singlepass) 137.832 ms (about 2.1x and 2.5x, derived from page data). prime-sieve: 14.390 ms vs Wasmtime cranelift 125.107 ms, Wasmtime winch 54.295 ms, Wasmer singlepass 57.379 ms (about 8.7x, 3.8x, 4.0x, derived from page data). minimal: 113.743 us vs Wasmtime cranelift 935.241 us (about 8.2x) but only 1.13x ahead of Wasmer singlepass 128.467 us (derived from page data). Compile time on pinky: 167.553 us vs Wasmtime cranelift 62.212 ms (about 370x); prime-sieve 442.354 us vs 76.662 ms (about 173x) (derived from page data). Steady-state execution is not faster: pinky 6.422 ms vs Wasmtime cranelift 5.776 ms; prime-sieve 2.104 ms vs 2.161 ms (parity); minimal 4.852 us vs 0.252 us per call (PolkaVM about 19x slower, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Numbers date from November 2024 (commit 190ea5ac; Wasmtime 26, Wasmer 5), long before current Wasmtime releases. This is a first-party suite: the PolkaVM author chose the workloads. The VMs execute different binaries (RISC-V for PolkaVM, Wasm for the rest), and the Wasm guests were built for the MVP target with sign-ext disabled. The win is in one-shot and compile time. Wasmtime cranelift is faster or equal in steady-state execution on pinky and prime-sieve, and about 19x faster per call on the minimal program, because PolkaVM's recompiler has a high fixed per-call cost from running in a separate sandbox process. Part of the compile-time gap is that Wasmtime cranelift optimizes while PolkaVM's recompiler is single-pass (README: guaranteed single-pass O(n) compilation). Wasmtime was built without parallel compilation. The README says the project is unfinished and should not be used in production.

notes: The numbers match BENCHMARKS.md exactly. The record's toolchain was HEAD's (1.86.0), not the benchmarked commit's (benchtool 1.82.0, guests nightly-2024-11-01); I fixed it and added the minimal-program rows, where PolkaVM's per-call execution is about 19x slower than Wasmtime. The metadata checks out: 434 stars, MIT OR Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-10-06, crates.io 9,754,111 downloads. Shortcomings to record: a first-party suite, a 2024 snapshot, the win is one-shot and compile time only, steady-state execution is equal to or slower than Wasmtime cranelift, and the README says not for production.

The execution win is also reproduced by an independent user suite (xusenlin/go-anydoc bench_test.go: Go 1.26.1, CGO_ENABLED=0, Apple M5 Pro, wazy v0.3.0 vs wazero v1.12.0, about 1.8x interpreted). That pinned third-party run is what holds A; the in-repo figures have a baseline-pin problem (see notes).

Compiled execution: string_manipulation -18%, reverse_array -14%, base64 -12%, fibonacci a wash. Host calls a tie (47.8 ns vs 48.3 ns). corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 (Go 1.26.1 on the go-anydoc third-party run, CGO_ENABLED=0); benchstat over interleaved A/B runs with upstream wazero as a control; commands: cd benchmarks/vs-wazero && go test -run='^$' -bench=. -benchmem -count=10. That module links wasmtime-go v34 and therefore needs cgo for every arm (docs/performance.md), so the head-to-head was not a CGO_ENABLED=0 build. The wazero pin is ambiguous: the benchmark README says fork point c0f3a4ec6411, docs/performance.md says f4779551afb4, and go.mod pins v1.12.1-0.20260904184217-6edbb8c01a5f; some figures were taken against wazero@main or wazero HEAD.
corrections.caveats: The baseline is wazero, not Wasmtime, Wasmer, WAMR or V8. docs/performance.md shows wazy behind Wasmtime Cranelift: about 16% behind on Case3/fibonacci, and 0.75 s vs 0.37 s (about 2x behind) on the 7.5 MB PDF run of the 6.5 MB module, where wazero took 3.4 s. It is ahead only on dynaddr (1.18x) and at parity on dispatch, and wazy omits the Spectre index clamping that Wasmtime does by default. The README itself says its largest figures (9.8x, 4.9x) come mostly from what WithCloseOnContextDone costs wazero, and that the raw code-generator gap is about 30% on the large module. The host-call and fibonacci results are ties. The README's Instantiate figure (9.1x, 3.3 KB heap per instance) comes from an engineering-log sweep on the pooled linear-memory path. On 2026-09-20 two correctness and isolation fixes landed on that path (commit ed4381b8 'stop recycling a memory a closed module can still reach', commit 0f363441 'stop racing api.Memory readers when a module closes'). The figure was not re-measured after them, and the wazero pin it ran against is not recorded. The project is a young single-author hard fork of wazero (not a GitHub fork) with 44 stars.

notes: The numbers are on the README, but 'compiled execution 4-18% (geomean about 6%)' is not on the page; I replaced it with the README values. reject_reason: other: invalid evidence. The only baseline comparison (the PolkaVM benchtool compile-time rows) times wazero's in-memory compiled-module cache instead of compilation: only the first of each batch of count CompileModule calls actually compiles.
tier_reason: The numbers are on BENCHMARKS.md, but the measurement is invalid. The benchtool Go shim (tools/benchtool/wazero/main.go at 190ea5ac, wazero v1.8.1) never calls CompiledModule.Close; Module_drop only removes a map entry. benchmark_compilation in tools/benchtool/src/main.rs calls compile count times on one runtime. wazero v1.8.1 runtime.CompileModule then hashes the binary into module.ID, and engine.CompileModule returns early on a compiledModules[module.ID] hit (internal/engine/wazevo/engine.go: 'cache hit!'). So every iteration after the first measures only decode + validate + sha256 + map lookup, while Wasmtime and Wasmer recompile each time.

corrections.claimed_speedup: None valid. BENCHMARKS.md lists wazero compile times of 2.543 ms (pinky), 4.049 ms (prime-sieve) and 197.802 us (minimal) vs Wasmtime cranelift 62.212 ms / 76.662 ms / 858.096 us. These are mostly cached-module hits after decode and validation, not compilations: the shim never closes the CompiledModule, so wazero's in-memory cache keyed by the sha256 module ID serves repeat compiles of the same blob. There are no oneshot or execution rows for wazero.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Harness: Rust benchtool at commit 190ea5ac (Rust 1.82.0, cargo --release, lto = true, codegen-units = 1) loading a Go c-shared library (tools/benchtool/wazero, go build -buildmode=c-shared; go.mod pins github.com/tetratelabs/wazero v1.8.1, go directive 1.21.3; Go toolchain version not stated). Default wazero.NewRuntime (compiler engine on amd64).
corrections.caveats: The only third-party comparison is invalid as a compile-time measurement. The PolkaVM benchtool shim never calls CompiledModule.Close, so repeated CompileModule calls on one runtime hit wazero's in-memory compiled-module cache, and only the first iteration compiles. The run used wazero v1.8.1 (November 2024). wazero's own README makes no claim against another runtime; it only says its compiler is often 10x faster than its interpreter. The repository now lives at github.com/wazero/wazero (tetratelabs/wazero redirects there).

notes: Reject for invalid evidence. This follows the MQF no-op precedent: the timed loop skips the work it claims to measure. I traced it through the shim's main.go (no Close), benchtool's benchmark_compilation (count compiles per engine) and the cache-hit early return in wazero v1.8.1 engine.CompileModule. If the orchestrator keeps wazero, it should be as an incumbent baseline with no faster-than claim. The metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 6.4k stars, last commit 2026-09-28. The canonical repo is now wazero/wazero.
